Title:
The Clarification Procedure
Introduction

Suspended matter in raw water supplies is removed by various methods to 
 provide a water suitable for domestic purposes and most industrial 
 requirements. Removal is generally accomplished by coagulation, flocculation 
 and sedimentation. The combination of these three processes is referred to as 
 conventional clarification.

Coagulation is the process of "destabilization by charge neutralization". Once 
 neutralized, particles no longer repel each other and can be brought 
 together. Coagulation is necessary for the removal of the colloidal-sized 
 suspended matter.

Flocculation is the process of bringing together the destabilized or 
 "coagulated" particles to form a larger agglomeration or "floc".

Sedimentation refers to the physical removal from suspension, or settling, 
 that occurs once the particles have been coagulated and flocculated. 
 Sedimentation or subsidence alone, without prior coagulation results in the 
 removal of relatively coarse suspended solids only.

Steps of Clarification

Finely divided particles suspended in surface water repel each other because 
 their surfaces are predominantly negatively charged.

Clarification involves the following steps to allow the particles to 
 agglomerate:
Coagulation

Use of inorganic salts of aluminum or iron which neutralize the charge on 
 the turbidity-particle. These also hydrolyze to form insoluble precipitates, 
 which entrap additional particles.

Use of a water-soluble organic polymers with numerous 'ionized sites for 
 particle charge neutralization.

sections.text: Flocculation

Flocculation, the agglomeration of destabilized particles into large 
 particles, can be enhanced by the addition of high molecular-weight, 
 water-soluble organic polymers, which increase floc size by charged site 
 binding and by molecular bridging.
Inorganic Coagulants

Table1- lists a number of common inorganic coagulants. Except for 
 sodium aluminate, all common iron and aluminum coagulants are acid salts which 
 lower the pH of the treated water by hydrolysis. Depending on initial raw 
 water alkalinity and pH, an alkali such as lime or caustic must be added to 
 counteract the pH depression of the primary or inorganic coagulant.

Because pH can affect both particle surface charge and floc precipitation 
 during coagulation, it is an extremely important variable. Iron and aluminum 
 hydroxide flocs are best precipitated at pH levels which minimize the 
 hydroxide solubility. However, the best pH for coagulating suspended solids 
 does not always coincide with the optimum pH for minimum hydroxide floc 
 solubility.

With aluminum sulfate, the optimum coagulation efficiency and minimum floc 
 solubility normally occur at pH 6.0 to 7.0. Sodium aluminate, being alkaline 
 is best used at elevated pH's, such as are encountered in precipitation 
 softening. Iron coagulants can be used successfully over the much broader pH 
 range of 5.0 to 11.0. But when ferrous compounds are used, oxidation to ferric 
 iron is needed for complete precipitation. This may require either 
 chlorination or pH levels greater than 8.0.

sections.text: Polyelectrolytes

The term polyelectrolyte refers to all water-soluble organic polymers used for 
 clarification, whether they function as primary coagulants or flocculants.
Water-soluble polymers available may be classified as follows:

items:
Anionic-ionize in water solution to form negative sites along the polymer 
 molecule,
Cationic-ionize to form positive sites,

Nonionic-ionize in water to form very slight negatively charged sites along 
 the polymer chain.

sections.text:
Polymeric primary coagulants are cationic materials with relatively low 
 molecular-weights (less than 500,000). The cationic charge density (available 
 positively charged sites) is very high. Polymeric flocculants or coagulant 
 aids may be anionic, cationic, or nonionic. Their molecular weights will range 
 up to 50,000,000. They function primarily by bridging particles together.

For any given particle there is an ideal molecular weight and an ideal charge 
 density for optimum coagulation. Further, there is an optimum charge and 
 molecular weight for the most efficient flocculants.

Since suspensions are normally nonuniform, specific testing is necessary to 
 find the coagulants and flocculants with the broadest range of performance.
Primary Coagulant Polyelectrolytes

Cationic polyelectrolyte commonly used as primary coagulants are polyamines. 
 They exhibit strong cationic ionization and have relatively low molecular 
 weights of less than 500,000. When used as primary coagulants, they adsorb on 
 particle surfaces, thus neutralizing the repelling negative charges. The 
 polymer may also bridge, for some extent, from one particle to another. This 
 accomplishes clarification and flocculation without the requirement for 
 precipitation of additional suspended solids by inorganic coagulants. The pH 
 of the treated water is unaffected.

The efficiency of primary coagulant polyelectrolytes depends greatly on the 
 exact nature of the turbidity particles to be coagulated, the amount of 
 turbidity present, and the turbulence available during coagulation. With lower 
 influent turbidities, more turbulence or mixing is required to achieve maximum 
 charge neutralizations.
Fig 1 Clarifier and Zones

The difference in clarifier sludge volume is 
 shown in two cones. Typically, polymer sludge volume (right) is 30 to 70% less 
 than that with alum treatment (left) as shown in figure1.

Raw waters of less than 10 Nephelometric 
 Turbidity Units (NTU) usually cannot be clarified with a cationic polymer 
 alone. Best results are obtained by a "combination of an inorganic salt 
 and cationic polymer".

With greater than 60 NTU turbidity, the use of a 
 primary coagulant polymer alone is normally sufficient.

Another treatment approach can be used on 
 low-turbidity waters where it is desirable to avoid using an inorganic 
 coagulant, artificial turbidity in the form of bentonite clay can be added to 
 build floc. The addition of a clay provides additional surface area for 
 adsorption and entrapment of finely divided turbidity. A polymeric coagulant 
 is added to complete the coagulation process.

A few of the advantages of the organic 
 polymer-type coagulants are:

items:
The volume of sludge produced 
 during clarification 
 can be reduced by 50 to 90%.

The resulting sludge contains 
 less water and can be more easily dewatered.

Polymeric coagulants do not 
 affect pH. The need for an alkaline chemical such as lime, caustic or soda 
 ash is thereby reduced or eliminated.

Polymeric coagulants do not add 
 to the total dissolved solids concentration. For example, alum adds 0.45 ppm 
 of sulfate ion (as CaCO3) for each ppm of commercial alum used. 
 The reduction in sulfate may significantly extend the capacity of 
 anion exchange systems.

Soluble iron or aluminum 
 carryover in the clarifier effluent may result from inorganic coagulant use. 
 Therefore, elimination of the inorganic coagulant can minimize the 
 deposition of these metals in filters, ion exchange units, and cooling 
 systems.

sections.text: Coagulant Aids (Flocculants)

In certain instances, an excess of primary coagulant, whether inorganic, 
 polymeric or a combination of both is fed to promote large floc size and 
 settling rate. A polymeric coagulant aid added after the primary coagulant 
 can, by developing a dense floc at low treatment levels, reduce the amount of 
 primary coagulant required.

Coagulant aids also broaden the pH range over which satisfactory; coagulation 
 may occur. In-Addition they can be-used to eliminate floc carryover from the 
 sedimentation unit. Generally, very high molecular weight, slight anionic 
 polyacrylamides are the most effective coagulant aids. Nonionic or cationic 
 types have proven successful in some clarifier systems. Essentially, the 
 polymer bridges the small floc particles and causes them to agglomerate 
 rapidly into bigger and more cohesive flocs which settles quickly.
Color Reduction

Frequently, the objective of clarification is the reduction of color. Swamps 
 and wetlands introduce color into surface waters, particularly after heavy 
 rainfalls. Color can cause various problems such as objectionable taste, 
 increased bacteria and algae growth, fouling of anion exchange resins and 
 interference with coagulation and stabilization of soluble iron and 
 manganese.

Most organic color in surface waters is colloidal and negatively charged. 
 Chemically, color-producing compounds are classified as humic and fulvic 
 acids. Color can be removed by chlorination and coagulation with aluminum or 
 iron salts. Chlorine will oxidize color compounds while the inorganic 
 coagulants can physically remove many types of organic color by neutralization 
 of surface charges. Further color removal is obtained by chemical interaction 
 with aluminum or iron hydrolysis products. Cationic organic polyelectrolytes 
 can also coagulate some types of color particles

Coagulation for color reduction is normally carried out at pH 4.5 to 5.5. 
 Optimum pH for turbidity removal is usually much higher than that for color 
 reduction. The sulfate ions can interfere with coagulation for color 
 reduction, whereas calcium and magnesium ions can improve the process and 
 broaden the pH range in which color may be reduced effectively.
Conventional Clarification Equipment

The coagulation, flocculation and sedimentation process requires three 
 distinct unit processes;

items: Rapid mix for coagulation.
Moderate mixing for flocculation.
Floc and water separation.

sections.text: Horizontal Flow Clarifiers

Originally, conventional clarification units consisted of large, rectangular, 
 concrete basins divided into two or three sections. Each stage of the 
 clarification process occurred in one section of the basin. Water flow was 
 horizontal through such systems.

Horizontal flow units are still used in very large industrial plants and for 
 clarifying municipal water since the design is suited to large capacity 
 basins. The retention time is normally long, (up to 4 to 6 hr), and is chiefly 
 devoted to settling. Rapid mix is typically designed for 3 to 5 minutes and 
 slow mix for 15 to 30 minutes. This design affords great flexibility in 
 establishing proper chemical addition points. Also, such units are relatively 
 insensitive to sudden changes in water throughput.

Likewise, the long retention allows sufficient reaction time to make necessary 
 adjustments in chemical and polymer feed if raw water conditions suddenly 
 change. However, for all but very large treated water demands, horizontal 
 units require high construction costs and more land space per unit of water 
 capacity.
Upflow Clarifiers

Compact and relatively economical, upflow clarifiers accommodate coagulation, 
 flocculation and sedimentation in a single (usually circular) steel or
 concrete tank. These clarifiers are termed "upflow" because the water 
 flows up while the suspended solids settle. A key feature in maintaining a 
 high-clarity effluent is increased solids concrete through internal sludge 
 recirculation.

Because retention time in an upflow unit is approximately 1 to 2 hr, upflow 
 basins can be much smaller in size or holding capacity than horizontal basins 
 of equal throughput capacity. A rise rate of 0.70 to 1.25 gpm/ ft2 
 of surface area is normal for clarification. Combination 
 softening-clarification units may operate up to 1.5 gpm/ft2 per of 
 surface area due to particle size and densities of precipitated hardness

The throughput efficiency of upflow units is achieved by maximizing the linear 
 overflow weir length while minimizing the opportunity for short-circuiting 
 through the settling zone. In addition, the two mixing stages for coagulation 
 and flocculation occur within the same clarification tank.

Although upflow units may provide more efficient sedimentation than horizontal 
 designs, many upflow clarifiers compromise on the rapid and slow mix 
 sequences. Some types provide rapid, mechanical mixing and rely on flow 
 turbulence for flocculation; others eliminate the rapid mix stage and provide 
 only moderate turbulence for flocculation. However, in most cases, rapid mix 
 deficiencies can be over-come by adding the primary coagulant farther upstream 
 of the clarifier.
Sludge Blanket and Solids-Contact Clarification

Most upflow designs are called either "sludge blanket" or "solids-contact" 
 clarifiers. After coagulation and/or flocculation in the sludge blanket units, 
 the incoming water passes through the suspended layer of previously formed 
 floc. Figure (2) shows an upflow sludge blanket clarifier.

Because the center in these units is often shaped like an inverted cone, the 
 rise rate of the water decreases as it rises through the steadily enlarging 
 cross section. When the rise rate decreases enough to exactly equal the 
 settling rate of the suspended floc, a distinct sludge/liquid interface will 
 form.

Sludge blanket efficiency depends on the filtering action as the freshly 
 coagulated or flocculated water passes through the suspended floc. Higher 
 sludge levels increase the filtration efficiency. In practice, the top sludge 
 interface is carried it in highest safe level to avoid upsets which might 
 result in large amounts of floc carryover into the overflow. Likewise, 
 excessive sludge withdrawal or blowdown should be avoided. The sludge blanket 
 level is often highly sensitive to changes in throughoutput, coagulant 
 addition and changes in raw water chemistry and temperature.

Solids-contact refers to units in which large volumes of sludge are circulated 
 internally. The term solids-contact also describes the sludge blanket unit and 
 simply means that prior to and during sedimentation the chemically treated 
 water contacts previously coagulated solids. Solids-contact units often 
 combine both clarification and precipitation softening. Bringing the incoming 
 raw water into contact with recirculated sludge improves the efficiency of the 
 softening reactions, and increases the size and density of the floc particles.
In-Line Clarification

In-line clarification is the process of raw water turbidity removal by 
 coagulant addition just prior to filtration. Polyelectrolytes and/or inorganic 
 coagulants are fed to improve filtration efficiency and run length. Polymers 
 are favored since they do not add additional suspended solids loading which 
 would necessarily decrease run length.

Equipment design may be downflow or upflow, depending on raw water turbidity 
 and particle size. The downflow dual-media unit generally consists of layers 
 of various grades of anthracite and sand supported on a gravel bed. After 
 backwashing, the larger anthracite particles separate to the top of the bed, 
 while the more dense, smaller particles are at the bottom. The purpose is to 
 allow bed penetration of the floc, which reduces the potential for excessive 
 pressure drops due to blinding off the top portion of filter media. Thus, 
 higher filtration rates are realized without a significant loss in effluent 
 quality due to the feature of increased bed use. Normal filtration rates are 5 
 to 6 gpm/ft2.

Coagulant Selection and Feeding for In-Line 
Clarification

The choice of a polymer coagulant and feed rate 
 depends on equipment design and influent water turbidity. Initially, in-line 
 clarification was used in the treatment of low turbidity waters, but it is now 
 being utilized on many types of surface waters. On most waters, the use of a 
 cationic polymer coagulant alone is satisfactory. However, the addition of a 
 high-molecular-weight, cationic acrylamide copolymer may improve filtration 
 efficiency.

Polymer feed rates (ppm) are usually less than those used in conventional 
 clarification given the same raw water characteristics. Complete charge 
 neutralization and bridging is not necessary and should be avoided. Total 
 coagulation or flocculation may promote excessive entrapment of suspended 
 solids in the first portion of the filter media. This can cause blinding over 
 of the media, high pressure drops and short operating runs.

Polymer is applied only to provide sufficient neutralization to allow 
 entire-bed often and adsorption of particles through the entire bed. Often, 
 polymer feed rates are regulated by trial and error on the actual units to 
 minimize effluent turbidity and maximize service run length. Since optimum 
 flocculation is undesirable, polymer are injected just upstream of the units. 
 Normally, a short mixing period is required to achieve the degree of reaction 
 most suitable for unit operation. Dilution water may lie recommended to 
 disperse the polymer throughout the incoming water. However, it may lie 
 necessary to move the polymer injection point several times to improve 
 turbidity removal. Due to the nature of operation, a change of polymer feed 
 rate will typically show a change in effluent turbidity in relatively short 
 periods of time.
Coagulation Testing

Raw water analyses alone are not very useful to predict coagulation 
 conditions. Coagulation chemicals and appropriate dosages must be selected 
 either by operating experience with a given raw water or by simulation or the 
 clarification step on a laboratory scale.

Jar testing best simulates clarification chemistry and operation. A 
 multiple-paddle, beaker arrangement permits comparing various chemical 
 combinations, all of which are subjected to identical hydraulic conditions. 
 The effects of rapid and slow mix intensity and duration may also be observed. 
 Besides determining the optimum chemical program, the correct order of 
 addition may be established. The most critical measurements in the jar test 
 are coagulant and or flocculants dosages, pH, floc size and settling 
 characteristics, floc-forming time and finished water clarity. The effect of 
 sludge recirculation may be simulated by adding the sludge formed in one 
 series of jar tests to the next jar test. Results of jar tests are only 
 relative and frequent adjustments are necessary in full-scale plant operation.

Zeta potential measurements have been used experimentally to predict coagulant 
 requirements and optimum pH levels. Because the measurement require special 
 apparatus and a skilled technician, zeta potential has never become practical 
 for controlling industrial water clarification plants.
Chemical Additions

Although the most efficient sequence for 
 adding coagulation chemicals will vary depending on the type of water and 
 system used and must be checked by jar testing, it will usually be:

items: Chlorine,
Bentonite (for low turbidity waters),
Primary inorganic and /or polymer coagulant,
pH-adjusting chemicals,
Coagulant aid.

sections.text:
Chlorine may assist coagulation by oxidizing organic contaminants which have 
 dispersing properties, some waters having high organic content will require 
 increased primary coagulant demand. Chlorination prior to primary coagulant 
 will also reduce the coagulant dosage. When using inorganic coagulant, adding 
 pH-adjusting chemicals prior to the coagulant will establish the proper pH 
 environment for the primary coagulant.

All treatment chemicals (except coagulant aids should be added during very 
 turbulent mixing of the influent water. Rapid mixing while the aluminum and 
 iron coagulants are added ensures uniform action adsorption onto the suspended 
 matter.

High shear mixing is especially important when using cationic polymers as 
 primary coagulants In general, it is advisable to feed them as far ahead of 
 the clarifier as possible. However, high shear mixing must be avoided when a 
 coagulant aid is added to prevent interference with the polymer's bridging 
 function. Only moderate turbulence is needed to obtain floc growth.

 level is often highly sensitive to changes in throughoutput, coagulant 
 addition and changes in raw water chemistry and temperature.
Solids-contact refers to units in which large volumes of sludge are circulated 
 internally. The term solids-contact also describes the sludge blanket unit and 
 simply means that prior to and during sedimentation the chemically treated 
 water contacts previously coagulated solids. Solids-contact units often 
 combine both clarification and precipitation softening. Bringing the incoming 
 raw water into contact with recirculated sludge improves the efficiency of the 
 softening reactions, and increases the size and density of the floc particles.
In-Line Clarification
In-line clarification is the process of raw water turbidity removal by 
 coagulant addition just prior to filtration. Polyelectrolytes and/or inorganic 
 coagulants are fed to improve filtration efficiency and run length. Polymers 
 are favored since they do not add additional suspended solids loading which 
 would necessarily decrease run length.
Equipment design may be downflow or upflow, depending on raw water turbidity 
 and particle size. The downflow dual-media unit generally consists of layers 
 of various grades of anthracite and sand supported on a gravel bed. After 
 backwashing, the larger anthracite particles separate to the top of the bed, 
 while the more dense, smaller particles are at the bottom. The purpose is to 
 allow bed penetration of the floc, which reduces the potential for excessive 
 pressure drops due to blinding off the top portion of filter media. Thus, 
 higher filtration rates are realized without a significant loss in effluent 
 quality due to the feature of increased bed use. Normal filtration rates are 5 
 to 6 gpm/ft2.
Coagulant Selection and Feeding for In-Line 
Clarification
The choice of a polymer coagulant and feed rate 
 depends on equipment design and influent water turbidity. Initially, in-line 
 clarification was used in the treatment of low turbidity waters, but it is now 
 being utilized on many types of surface waters. On most waters, the use of a 
 cationic polymer coagulant alone is satisfactory. However, the addition of a 
 high-molecular-weight, cationic acrylamide copolymer may improve filtration 
 efficiency.
Polymer feed rates (ppm) are usually less than those used in conventional 
 clarification given the same raw water characteristics. Complete charge 
 neutralization and bridging is not necessary and should be avoided. Total 
 coagulation or flocculation may promote excessive entrapment of suspended 
 solids in the first portion of the filter media. This can cause blinding over 
 of the media, high pressure drops and short operating runs.
Polymer is applied only to provide sufficient neutralization to allow 
 entire-bed often and adsorption of particles through the entire bed. Often, 
 polymer feed rates are regulated by trial and error on the actual units to 
 minimize effluent turbidity and maximize service run length. Since optimum 
 flocculation is undesirable, polymer are injected just upstream of the units. 
 Normally, a short mixing period is required to achieve the degree of reaction 
 most suitable for unit operation. Dilution water may lie recommended to 
 disperse the polymer throughout the incoming water. However, it may lie 
 necessary to move the polymer injection point several times to improve 
 turbidity removal. Due to the nature of operation, a change of polymer feed 
 rate will typically show a change in effluent turbidity in relatively short 
 periods of time.
Coagulation Testing
Raw water analyses alone are not very useful to predict coagulation 
 conditions. Coagulation chemicals and appropriate dosages must be selected 
 either by operating experience with a given raw water or by simulation or the 
 clarification step on a laboratory scale.
Jar testing best simulates clarification chemistry and operation. A 
 multiple-paddle, beaker arrangement permits comparing various chemical 
 combinations, all of which are subjected to identical hydraulic conditions. 
 The effects of rapid and slow mix intensity and duration may also be observed. 
 Besides determining the optimum chemical program, the correct order of 
 addition may be established. The most critical measurements in the jar test 
 are coagulant and or flocculants dosages, pH, floc size and settling 
 characteristics, floc-forming time and finished water clarity. The effect of 
 sludge recirculation may be simulated by adding the sludge formed in one 
 series of jar tests to the next jar test. Results of jar tests are only 
 relative and frequent adjustments are necessary in full-scale plant operation.
Zeta potential measurements have been used experimentally to predict coagulant 
 requirements and optimum pH levels. Because the measurement require special 
 apparatus and a skilled technician, zeta potential has never become practical 
 for controlling industrial water clarification plants.
Chemical Additions
Although the most efficient sequence for 
 adding coagulation chemicals will vary depending on the type of water and 
 system used and must be checked by jar testing, it will usually be:
Chlorine,
Bentonite (for low turbidity waters),
Primary inorganic and /or polymer coagulant,
pH-adjusting chemicals,
Coagulant aid.
Chlorine may assist coagulation by oxidizing organic contaminants which have 
 dispersing properties, some waters having high organic content will require 
 increased primary coagulant demand. Chlorination prior to primary coagulant 
 will also reduce the coagulant dosage. When using inorganic coagulant, adding 
 pH-adjusting chemicals prior to the coagulant will establish the proper pH 
 environment for the primary coagulant.
All treatment chemicals (except coagulant aids should be added during very 
 turbulent mixing of the influent water. Rapid mixing while the aluminum and 
 iron coagulants are added ensures uniform action adsorption onto the suspended 
 matter.
High shear mixing is especially important when using cationic polymers as 
 primary coagulants In general, it is advisable to feed them as far ahead of 
 the clarifier as possible. However, high shear mixing must be avoided when a 
 coagulant aid is added to prevent interference with the polymer's bridging 
 function. Only moderate turbulence is needed to obtain floc growth.
